Sample Testing in Clinical Biochemistry: MCQs

faq.a: Serum is obtained after clotting, releasing intracellular potassium from platelets; plasma avoids this.
faq.q: Why is serum potassium higher than plasma potassium?

faq.a: Arterial or venous blood placed in a fluoride‑oxalate tube and analysed within 15 minutes.
faq.q: What is the best sample for measuring lactate in shock?

faq.a: Use a small gauge needle, avoid excessive tourniquet time, and gently invert tubes.
faq.q: How can I minimise hemolysis when drawing blood?

exam: A patient with severe malaria presents with jaundice – which biochemistry test will differentiate hemolysis from hepatic failure? — Check serum bilirubin fractions; predominance of unconjugated bilirubin points to hemolysis.

You receive a serum potassium of 6.2 mmol/L but the sample is visibly hemolysed – what is your next step? — Repeat the test using plasma or a fresh sample; treat only if repeat confirms hyperkalaemia.
In a rural clinic, the centrifuge is broken. How would you obtain a reliable glucose result for a comatose child? — Use a point‑of‑care capillary glucose meter on a finger‑stick sample.

A HIV‑positive patient has rising creatinine and proteinuria. Which two tests help stage renal involvement? — Serum creatinine for GFR estimation and urine dipstick for protein; consider urine microscopy if available.

During a blood draw for liver function tests, the tube is left at 37 °C for 2 hours. Which result is most likely affected? — AST and ALT may be falsely elevated due to enzyme degradation; repeat the test.

A child with sickle‑cell disease has a sudden drop in haemoglobin and high LDH. Which single test confirms an acute hemolytic crisis? — Serum potassium (often elevated) and LDH together; repeat CBC to document drop.
What quality‑control measure ensures analyzer accuracy daily? — Run low and high internal QC samples with each batch and compare to target ranges.
A patient on diuretics shows low sodium 128 mmol/L. How do you distinguish true hyponatraemia from lab error? — Verify sample integrity, repeat serum sodium, and assess clinical volume status.
ai.title: Sample Testing in Clinical Biochemistry
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Guides students through pre‑analytical, analytical and post‑analytical steps of common biochemistry tests in low‑resource settings, focusing on clinical reasoning and problem‑solving.

b: Pre‑analytical errors are the most common cause of inaccurate results.
Low‑resource labs may lack refrigeration or centrifuges.
sections.p: Biochemistry tests rely on proper specimen collection, transport and storage. Errors at any stage can mislead diagnosis, especially where test panels are limited.

b: Serum: clotting tube, 30 min at room temperature, then centrifuge.
Plasma: anticoagulant tube, immediate centrifuge if possible.
sections.p: Samples (blood, urine, CSF) are collected in specific tubes, processed to separate plasma/serum, and analysed by automated chemistry analyzers or point‑of‑care devices.

b: Internal QC runs with each batch.
External quality assessment participation when available.
sections.p: National laboratory standards (e.g., WHO SLIPTA) require documented SOPs, quality control, and regular equipment maintenance.

b: Prolonged storage can lower glucose and increase lactate.
sections.p: Hemolysis, delayed processing, temperature excursions, and wrong tube use cause spurious results.

b: Elevated bilirubin with hemolysis suggests malaria or sickle cell.
Low sodium in severe diarrhoea requires prompt correction.
sections.p: Accurate biochemistry results guide management of common tropical conditions such as malaria‑induced hemolysis, HIV‑related renal disease, and sickle‑cell crises.
When a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates (e.g., bedside capillary glucose for hypoglycaemia, urine colour for bilirubin).

t.b: Is the patient at risk of cardiac arrhythmia? – High >5.5 mmol/L indicates hemolysis or renal failure; low <3.5 mmol/L suggests diarrhoea or diuretics.
Is there acute kidney injury? – >133 µmol/L (male) or >124 µmol/L (female) signals reduced GFR; trend matters.
Is hypoglycaemia causing altered consciousness? – <2.8 mmol/L urgent dextrose; >11 mmol/L suggests diabetes stress hyperglycaemia.
Is jaundice due to hemolysis or liver disease? – Predominant unconjugated >50 µmol/L points to hemolysis; conjugated rise suggests cholestasis.
Is there renal involvement in HIV or malaria? – +1 or more indicates glomerular damage; confirm with microscopy if possible.

b: If hemolysis suspected, recollect in a new tube and avoid vigorous shaking.
For hyperkalaemia, give calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, and consider dialysis if refractory.
sections.p: Correct the pre‑analytical error, treat the underlying condition, and repeat the test if needed.

b: Check plasma potassium if serum is high and sample is hemolysed.
sections.p: Distinguish true hyperkalaemia from pseudohyperkalaemia caused by platelet release in clotting serum.

b: Correlate labs with clinical picture before concluding organ failure.
sections.p: Severe dehydration can falsely elevate urea and creatinine; malaria‑induced hemolysis can raise LDH mimicking liver injury.

b: Always note sample type and time of collection.
Explain why a test may be unavailable and what alternative you would use.
sections.p: Focus on the chain of pre‑analytical, analytical and post‑analytical steps; know the most common errors and how to mitigate them in low‑resource settings.
